goals: Define hormones and locate the human endocrine glands
Explain how the hypothalamus controls the two lobes of the pituitary
State the hormones of the pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid and thymus with their actions
Relate growth hormone and thyroid disorders to their causes

slides.heading: Chemical Coordination and Integration
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the endocrine glands of the head, neck and chest, and the hormones they make.

visual.alt: Flow showing neural and endocrine systems together coordinating body functions

slides.narration: Nerve fibres do not reach every cell, and cellular functions need continuous regulation. So the neural system works together with a second system, the endocrine system, which sends chemical messages called hormones through the blood. Together they coordinate and integrate the activities of the organs.

slides.heading: Endocrine glands and hormones
slides.body_md: Endocrine glands lack ducts and are called **ductless glands**; their secretions are **hormones**. A hormone is a **non-nutrient chemical** which acts as an **intercellular messenger** and is produced in **trace amounts**.

rows: A surface or cavity through the duct
The blood, to distant target organs

visual.alt: Table comparing exocrine and endocrine glands

slides.narration: An exocrine gland pours its secretion through a duct. An endocrine gland has no duct, so its hormones enter the blood and reach target organs far away. Invertebrates have simple endocrine systems with few hormones, while vertebrates use many chemicals as hormones.

slides.heading: The human endocrine glands
slides.body_md: The organised glands are the **pituitary, pineal, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, parathyroid, thymus and gonads** (testis in males, ovary in females). The **hypothalamus**, and organs such as the gut, liver, kidney and heart, also produce hormones.

slides.narration: Find each gland on the outline. The hypothalamus and pituitary sit at the base of the brain, the pineal on the upper side of the forebrain, the thyroid and parathyroids in the neck, the thymus in the chest, the adrenals on the kidneys, the pancreas in the abdomen and the gonads lower down.

slides.heading: The hypothalamus
slides.body_md: The hypothalamus is the basal part of the **diencephalon** (forebrain). Groups of **neurosecretory cells** called **nuclei** make hormones that regulate the pituitary.

rows: Stimulates secretion of a pituitary hormone
GnRH stimulates synthesis and release of gonadotrophins
Inhibits secretion of a pituitary hormone
Somatostatin inhibits release of growth hormone

visual.alt: Table of releasing and inhibiting hormones of the hypothalamus with examples

slides.narration: These hormones start in hypothalamic neurons, travel along their axons and are released from the nerve endings. They then reach the pituitary through a portal circulation and regulate the anterior pituitary. The posterior pituitary is under direct neural control of the hypothalamus.

slides.heading: How the hypothalamus controls the pituitary

slides.heading: Hormones of the anterior pituitary
slides.body_md: The **pars distalis**, commonly called the anterior pituitary, produces six hormones.

rows: Growth of mammary glands and formation of milk
Synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones
Secretion of glucocorticoids by the adrenal cortex
Males: androgen secretion. Females: ovulation of the Graafian follicle and maintenance of the corpus luteum
Males: with androgens regulates spermatogenesis. Females: growth of ovarian follicles

visual.alt: Table of six anterior pituitary hormones and their actions

slides.narration: Several of these hormones control other glands, so the anterior pituitary is often called a master gland, though it is itself controlled by the hypothalamus. Luteinising and follicle stimulating hormones act on the gonads and are called gonadotrophins.

slides.heading: Pars intermedia and the posterior pituitary
slides.body_md: In humans the pars intermedia is almost merged with the pars distalis.

rows: Acts on melanocytes; regulates skin pigmentation
Made in the hypothalamus; released by the pars nervosa
Contracts smooth muscle: vigorous uterine contraction at childbirth, milk ejection
Made in the hypothalamus; released by the pars nervosa
Reabsorption of water and electrolytes by distal tubules; reduces diuresis

visual.alt: Table of MSH, oxytocin and vasopressin with sources and actions

slides.narration: When the synthesis or release of vasopressin is impaired, the kidney cannot conserve water. Large volumes of urine are lost and the body dehydrates. This condition is diabetes insipidus, which has nothing to do with sugar.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting pituitary hormones
slides.body_md: A student lists every hormone released by the three parts of the pituitary. How many are there, and how many of them are actually made in the pituitary?
bullets: Pars distalis 6 (GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH) + pars intermedia 1 (MSH) + pars nervosa 2: $6 + 1 + 2 = 9$.
Oxytocin and vasopressin are made in the hypothalamus, so $9 - 2 = 7$ are made in the pituitary itself.
The pars nervosa only **stores and releases** its two hormones.

visual.alt: Worked table: 9 pituitary hormones, 7 made in the gland

slides.narration: Six from the pars distalis, one from the pars intermedia and two from the pars nervosa make nine. But the last two are only stored there, having travelled down axons from the hypothalamus, so seven are made in the pituitary itself.

slides.heading: Growth hormone disorders
slides.body_md: Too much or too little growth hormone, at different ages, gives different disorders.

rows: Abnormal growth of the whole body
Excess GH in adults, especially in middle age
Severe disfigurement, especially of the face; serious complications and early death if unchecked; often undetected for years

visual.alt: Table of gigantism, pituitary dwarfism and acromegaly

slides.narration: Age decides the outcome. Before growth has stopped, extra growth hormone makes the whole body grow abnormally large. In middle age it causes acromegaly, with coarse facial features, which is hard to diagnose early and may go unnoticed for many years.

slides.heading: Pineal and thyroid glands
slides.body_md: The **pineal** lies on the dorsal side of the forebrain. The **thyroid** has two lobes on either side of the **trachea**, joined by an **isthmus**; it is made of **follicles** and stromal tissue.

rows: Regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm: sleep–wake cycle, body temperature; influences metabolism, pigmentation, menstrual cycle and defence capability
Regulate basal metabolic rate; support RBC formation; control metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats; maintain water and electrolyte balance
A protein hormone that regulates blood calcium

visual.alt: Table of pineal and thyroid hormones and their roles

slides.narration: Iodine is essential for the normal rate of thyroid hormone synthesis. Its deficiency causes hypothyroidism and an enlarged thyroid called goitre. Hypothyroidism in pregnancy causes cretinism in the baby. Thyroid cancer or nodules can cause hyperthyroidism, and exophthalmic goitre, or Graves disease, brings protruding eyeballs, a high metabolic rate and weight loss.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: iodine in thyroid hormones
slides.body_md: Thyroxine has 4 iodine atoms and triiodothyronine 3. (i) What percentage of thyroxine’s iodine is removed when it becomes triiodothyronine? (ii) With molar masses 777 (thyroxine) and 127 (iodine), what percentage of thyroxine’s mass is iodine?
bullets: (i) $\dfrac{4 - 3}{4} \times 100 = 25$ percent.
(ii) $\dfrac{4 \times 127}{777} \times 100 = \dfrac{508}{777} \times 100 \approx 65.4$ percent.
About two-thirds of the hormone’s mass is iodine, so a diet short of iodine quickly limits hormone synthesis.

rows: Iodine mass per mole of thyroxine

visual.alt: Worked table: 25 percent of iodine atoms removed; iodine about 65.4 percent of thyroxine by mass

slides.narration: Removing one of four iodine atoms removes a quarter of them, twenty-five percent. Four iodine atoms weigh about five hundred and eight units out of seven hundred and seventy-seven, about sixty-five percent of the molecule. No wonder iodine shortage lowers hormone output and leads to goitre.

slides.heading: Quick check: goitre
slides.body_md: Explain the neck swelling seen in an iodine-poor hill district.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which gland enlarges when iodine is short?

slides.heading: Parathyroid glands and thymus
slides.body_md: **Four parathyroid glands** lie on the back of the thyroid, one pair in each lobe. The **thymus** is a lobular structure between the lungs, behind the sternum, on the ventral side of the aorta.

rows: Raises blood calcium (hypercalcaemic): stimulates bone resorption, renal reabsorption of calcium and absorption of calcium from digested food; secretion regulated by blood calcium; with TCT keeps calcium balanced
Differentiation of T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity); promote antibody production (humoral immunity); thymus degenerates with age, so immunity weakens

visual.alt: Table of parathyroid hormone and thymosins with their roles

slides.narration: Parathyroid hormone dissolves calcium from bone, saves it in the kidney and absorbs more from food, so blood calcium rises. The thymus helps build the immune system; as it shrinks in old age, fewer thymosins are made and immune responses become weaker.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Hormones: non-nutrient intercellular messengers made in trace amounts by ductless glands.
Hypothalamus: releasing (GnRH) and inhibiting (somatostatin) hormones reach the anterior pituitary through the portal system; posterior pituitary under direct neural control.
Pars distalis: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH; pars intermedia: MSH; pars nervosa releases oxytocin and vasopressin made in the hypothalamus.
GH: gigantism, dwarfism, acromegaly. ADH lack: diabetes insipidus.
Pineal: melatonin and daily rhythms. Thyroid: T4, T3, TCT; goitre, cretinism, Graves’ disease.
Parathyroid: PTH raises calcium. Thymus: thymosins for T-lymphocytes.

rows: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH

visual.alt: Summary table of glands and key hormones in Part 1

slides.narration: To recap: the hypothalamus controls the pituitary through blood vessels and nerves. The pituitary releases nine hormones, two of them made in the hypothalamus. The pineal sets daily rhythms, the thyroid sets metabolic rate, the parathyroids raise calcium, and the thymus supports immunity.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Say that oxytocin and vasopressin are **made in the hypothalamus** and only **stored** in the posterior pituitary.
Separate **gigantism** (child), **dwarfism** (deficiency) and **acromegaly** (adult).
Do not confuse **diabetes insipidus** (ADH) with **diabetes mellitus** (insulin).
Link **iodine deficiency** to goitre and **cretinism**; **Graves’ disease** to hyperthyroidism.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Oxytocin and vasopressin are made in the hypothalamus. Match growth hormone disorders to age. Keep diabetes insipidus and diabetes mellitus apart. And link iodine to goitre and cretinism, but Graves disease to an overactive thyroid.

slides.body_md: Part 2 — glands of the abdomen and pelvis, hormones of other organs, and how hormones act on cells.

visual.alt: Flow from gland through blood and receptor to response

slides.narration: In this part we meet the adrenal glands, the pancreas and the gonads, then hormones from the heart, kidney and gut. Finally we see how a hormone, after reaching its target, binds a receptor and changes what the cell does.

slides.heading: Adrenal medulla: emergency hormones
slides.body_md: One adrenal gland sits on the anterior part of each kidney: a central **medulla** and an outer **cortex**. The medulla secretes **adrenaline (epinephrine)** and **noradrenaline (norepinephrine)**, the **catecholamines**.

rows: Faster heart beat, stronger contraction, faster breathing
Breakdown of glycogen (blood glucose rises), lipids and proteins

visual.alt: Table of the effects of adrenaline and noradrenaline

slides.narration: These hormones are secreted rapidly in response to any stress or emergency, so they are called emergency hormones, or hormones of fight or flight. Every effect prepares the body for sudden action, from a faster heart to more glucose in the blood.

slides.heading: Adrenal cortex: corticoids
slides.body_md: The cortex has three layers: **zona glomerulosa** (outer), **zona fasciculata** (middle) and **zona reticularis** (inner). Its hormones are the **corticoids**.

rows: Carbohydrate metabolism: gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, proteolysis; inhibit cellular uptake of amino acids; maintain heart and kidney function; anti-inflammatory; suppress immunity; stimulate RBC production
Renal tubules reabsorb sodium ions and water and excrete potassium and phosphate ions; maintain fluid volume, osmotic pressure and blood pressure
Growth of axial, pubic and facial hair at puberty

visual.alt: Table of the three groups of adrenal cortex hormones

slides.narration: Underproduction of cortex hormones alters carbohydrate metabolism and causes acute weakness and fatigue. This is Addison disease. Notice that cortisol both raises glucose production and calms inflammation, which is why cortisol-like medicines are used for swollen, inflamed tissue.

slides.heading: Quick check: adrenaline
slides.body_md: Which change is NOT caused by the emergency hormones?
slides.narration: Quick check. In fright, do the pupils widen or narrow?

slides.heading: Pancreas: insulin and glucagon
slides.body_md: The pancreas is a **composite gland**, both exocrine and endocrine. Its endocrine part is about **1 to 2 million islets of Langerhans**, only **1 to 2 percent** of the pancreatic tissue.

rows: Acts mainly on hepatocytes: glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; reduces cellular glucose uptake; raises blood glucose (hyperglycaemic)
Acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes: glucose uptake and use; glycogenesis; lowers blood glucose (hypoglycaemic)

visual.alt: Table of glucagon and insulin with their source cells and actions

slides.narration: Glucagon and insulin pull in opposite directions, keeping glucose within limits. Prolonged hyperglycaemia leads to diabetes mellitus, with loss of glucose in the urine and harmful ketone bodies. Diabetic patients are successfully treated with insulin therapy.

slides.heading: Blood glucose after a glucose drink
slides.body_md: In a healthy person insulin brings glucose back towards the fasting level within about two hours. Without enough insulin, glucose stays high, crosses the kidney threshold and appears in the urine.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: glucose in the blood
slides.body_md: An adult has about 5 litres of blood at 90 mg of glucose per dL. (i) How many grams of glucose are in the blood? (ii) After a glucose drink the level peaks at 140 mg per dL. What is the percentage rise?
bullets: (i) $5 \times 10 = 50$ dL; $90 \times 50 = 4500$ mg, that is 4.5 g.
(ii) $\dfrac{140 - 90}{90} \times 100 \approx 55.6$ percent.
Only a few grams circulate at any moment, so insulin and glucagon must adjust it constantly.

visual.alt: Worked table: 4.5 grams of glucose; peak rise about 55.6 percent

slides.narration: Five litres is fifty decilitres. Ninety milligrams in each gives four thousand five hundred milligrams, only four and a half grams of glucose in all the blood. A rise from ninety to one hundred and forty is about fifty-six percent, and in health insulin soon brings it back.

slides.heading: Testis and ovary
slides.body_md: The gonads are primary sex organs and endocrine glands.

rows: Androgens, mainly testosterone, from Leydig (interstitial) cells
Development and function of male accessory sex organs; muscular growth, facial and axillary hair, low-pitched voice, aggressiveness; spermatogenesis; male sexual behaviour (libido); anabolic effects
Growth of female secondary sex organs and follicles; female secondary sex characters such as high-pitched voice; mammary gland development; female sexual behaviour
Supports pregnancy; formation of alveoli in mammary glands and milk secretion

visual.alt: Table of testis and ovary hormones and roles

slides.narration: The testis is made of seminiferous tubules and interstitial tissue; Leydig cells in the spaces between tubules make androgens. The ovary produces one ovum in each menstrual cycle. After ovulation the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes mainly progesterone.

slides.heading: Hormones of the heart, kidney and gut
slides.body_md: Some organs that are not endocrine glands also secrete hormones.

rows: Dilates blood vessels; lowers raised blood pressure
Gastric glands secrete HCl and pepsinogen
Exocrine pancreas secretes water and bicarbonate ions
Pancreas releases enzymes; gall bladder releases bile

visual.alt: Table of hormones of the heart, kidney and gastrointestinal tract

slides.narration: Several other non-endocrine tissues secrete hormones called growth factors, needed for normal growth and repair. Notice how the four gut hormones coordinate digestion, switching secretions on and off as food moves along.

slides.heading: Quick check: blood pressure
slides.body_md: Which hormone would the heart secrete when blood pressure rises sharply?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which chamber wall makes it, and does it raise or lower pressure?

slides.heading: Chemical nature of hormones
slides.body_md: Hormones act through specific proteins called **hormone receptors**, found only in target tissues. **Membrane-bound** receptors lie on the cell membrane; **intracellular** receptors are mostly nuclear. Each receptor is specific to one hormone.

rows: Insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones

visual.alt: Table of four chemical classes of hormones with examples and receptor types

slides.narration: When a hormone binds its receptor, a hormone receptor complex forms and causes biochemical changes in the target tissue. Because receptors are specific, a hormone carried everywhere in the blood still acts only on its own target cells.

slides.heading: Mechanism of hormone action
slides.body_md: Membrane-receptor hormones generate **second messengers** (cyclic AMP, IP3, calcium ions). Intracellular-receptor hormones act on the **genome**, regulating **gene expression**.

On the right, a steroid or thyroid hormone enters the cell, binds a receptor in the nucleus and switches genes on or off, so new proteins are made more slowly.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: amplification and removal
slides.body_md: (i) One hormone molecule activates one receptor, which makes 100 cyclic AMP molecules; each leads to 50 product molecules. How many products? (ii) A hormone with a half-life of 10 minutes is released in one burst. What percentage remains after 30 minutes? (Illustrative numbers.)
bullets: (i) $1 \times 100 \times 50 = 5000$ product molecules.
(ii) $\dfrac{30}{10} = 3$ half-lives; $\dfrac{1}{8} \times 100 = 12.5$ percent remains.
Amplification explains how **trace amounts** work; quick removal lets the signal be switched off.

visual.alt: Worked table: 5000 products from one hormone; 12.5 percent left after three half-lives

slides.narration: One times one hundred times fifty gives five thousand product molecules from a single hormone molecule, which is why trace amounts are enough. Thirty minutes is three half-lives, so one half, then a quarter, then an eighth remains, twelve and a half percent.

slides.heading: Endocrine disorders
slides.body_md: Too much or too little of a hormone upsets body functions.

rows: Enlarged thyroid; stunted growth and mental retardation in babies
Protruding eyes, high BMR, weight loss
Hyperglycaemia, glucose in urine, ketone bodies

visual.alt: Table of endocrine disorders with hormone problems and features

slides.narration: Each disorder points back to one hormone. Ask whether there is too much or too little, and when it began. Growth hormone disorders depend on age, thyroid disorders on iodine and gland activity, and the two kinds of diabetes on two different hormones.

slides.heading: Quick check: second messengers
slides.body_md: Which hormone acts through a second messenger without entering its target cell?
slides.narration: Quick check. Peptides stay outside; steroids and thyroid hormones go in.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Adrenal medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline, fight or flight. Cortex (glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis): cortisol, aldosterone, androgens; Addison’s disease.
Pancreas: α cells glucagon (raises glucose), β cells insulin (lowers glucose); diabetes mellitus.
Testis: androgens from Leydig cells. Ovary: estrogen from follicles, progesterone from the corpus luteum.
ANF lowers blood pressure; erythropoietin makes RBCs; gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP coordinate digestion.
Receptors are specific: membrane-bound (second messengers) or intracellular (gene expression).

visual.alt: Summary table of the two receptor pathways

slides.narration: To recap: the adrenal medulla prepares us for emergencies while the cortex manages fuel, salt and water. Insulin and glucagon balance blood glucose. Gonads, heart, kidney and gut all release hormones. And every hormone acts through a specific receptor, either on the membrane or inside the cell.

bullets: Write **glycogenolysis** for glucagon and **glycogenesis** for insulin; do not swap them.
Name the **three cortex zones** in order and one hormone group from each role.
For mechanism questions, give the **four chemical classes** and the **two receptor pathways** with examples.
Learn the **four gut hormones** with their targets.

sections.heading: 1. Endocrine glands, hormones and the hypothalamus
sections.body_md:
Nerve fibres do not innervate every cell, and cellular functions need continuous regulation, so the **neural system** and the **endocrine system** jointly coordinate and integrate the activities of organs.

**Endocrine glands** lack ducts (**ductless glands**); their secretions are **hormones**. The present definition: a hormone is a **non-nutrient chemical** which acts as an **intercellular messenger** and is produced in **trace amounts**. Invertebrates have simple endocrine systems with few hormones; vertebrates use many chemicals as hormones.

The organised endocrine bodies of the human are the **pituitary, pineal, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, parathyroid, thymus and gonads** (testis in males, ovary in females). Other organs — the **gastrointestinal tract, liver, kidney and heart** — also produce hormones.

**Hypothalamus.** The basal part of the **diencephalon** (forebrain). It contains groups of **neurosecretory cells** called **nuclei**, which make hormones that regulate the synthesis and secretion of pituitary hormones:
- **Releasing hormones** stimulate pituitary secretion — e.g. **gonadotrophin releasing hormone (GnRH)** stimulates the synthesis and release of gonadotrophins.
- **Inhibiting hormones** inhibit it — e.g. **somatostatin** inhibits the release of growth hormone.

These hormones originate in hypothalamic neurons, pass through their axons and are released from the nerve endings. They reach the pituitary through a **portal circulatory system** (hypophysial portal system) and regulate the **anterior pituitary**. The **posterior pituitary** is under the **direct neural regulation** of the hypothalamus.

key_terms.definition_md: A non-nutrient chemical that acts as an intercellular messenger and is produced in trace amounts.
A hypothalamic hormone that stimulates pituitary secretion, such as GnRH.
A hypothalamic hormone that inhibits pituitary secretion, such as somatostatin.

sections.heading: 2. The pituitary gland
sections.body_md:
The pituitary lies in a bony cavity called the **sella turcica** and is attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk. It has two parts: the **adenohypophysis** (pars distalis and pars intermedia) and the **neurohypophysis** (pars nervosa).

**Pars distalis** (commonly the anterior pituitary):
- **Growth hormone (GH):** over-secretion causes **gigantism**; low secretion causes stunted growth, **pituitary dwarfism**. Excess in adults, especially in middle age, causes **acromegaly** — severe disfigurement, especially of the face, with serious complications and premature death if unchecked; it is hard to diagnose early and often goes undetected for years.
- **Prolactin (PRL):** growth of the mammary glands and formation of milk.
- **TSH:** synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones.
- **ACTH:** synthesis and secretion of glucocorticoids by the adrenal cortex.
- **LH and FSH (gonadotrophins):** in males LH stimulates androgen secretion from the testis, and FSH with androgens regulates spermatogenesis; in females LH induces ovulation of fully mature (Graafian) follicles and maintains the corpus luteum, and FSH stimulates growth of ovarian follicles.

**Pars intermedia:** only **MSH**, which acts on melanocytes and regulates skin pigmentation. In humans it is almost merged with the pars distalis.

**Neurohypophysis (pars nervosa, posterior pituitary):** stores and releases **oxytocin** and **vasopressin**, which are synthesised in the hypothalamus and transported axonally.
- **Oxytocin** contracts smooth muscle: vigorous uterine contraction at childbirth and milk ejection from the mammary glands.
- **Vasopressin (anti-diuretic hormone, ADH)** acts mainly on the kidney, stimulating **reabsorption of water and electrolytes by the distal tubules** and so reducing diuresis. Impaired synthesis or release of ADH reduces the kidney’s ability to conserve water, causing water loss and dehydration: **diabetes insipidus**.

Counting: 6 (pars distalis) + 1 (pars intermedia) + 2 (pars nervosa) = 9 hormones released, 7 of them made in the pituitary.

sections.heading: 3. Pineal, thyroid, parathyroid and thymus
sections.body_md:
**Pineal gland:** on the dorsal side of the forebrain; secretes **melatonin**, which regulates the **24-hour (diurnal) rhythm** — sleep–wake cycle and body temperature — and influences metabolism, pigmentation, the menstrual cycle and defence capability.

**Thyroid:** two lobes on either side of the **trachea**, joined by a thin flap of connective tissue, the **isthmus**. It is made of **follicles** and stromal tissue; each follicle has follicular cells around a cavity. Follicular cells make **tetraiodothyronine (thyroxine, T4)** and **triiodothyronine (T3)**. **Iodine** is essential for their normal rate of synthesis (thyroxine has 4 iodine atoms, triiodothyronine 3; iodine is about 65 percent of thyroxine’s mass). Thyroid hormones regulate the **basal metabolic rate**, support **RBC formation**, control the metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, and maintain water and electrolyte balance. The thyroid also secretes **thyrocalcitonin (TCT)**, a protein hormone that regulates blood calcium.
- **Iodine deficiency** → **hypothyroidism** and enlarged thyroid, **goitre**.
- Hypothyroidism **during pregnancy** → defective development of the baby: **cretinism** (stunted growth, mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin, deaf-mutism). In adult women it may make the menstrual cycle irregular.
- **Hyperthyroidism** (from thyroid cancer or nodules) raises hormone levels; **exophthalmic goitre (Graves’ disease)** shows an enlarged thyroid, protruding eyeballs, increased BMR and weight loss.

**Parathyroid:** **four glands** on the back of the thyroid, one pair in each lobe. They secrete the peptide **parathyroid hormone (PTH)**, regulated by circulating calcium ions. PTH **raises blood calcium** (**hypercalcaemic**): it stimulates **bone resorption** (demineralisation), **reabsorption of calcium by renal tubules** and **absorption of calcium from digested food**. With TCT it maintains calcium balance.

**Thymus:** a lobular structure between the lungs behind the sternum, on the ventral side of the aorta. It secretes peptide **thymosins**, which help **differentiate T-lymphocytes** (cell-mediated immunity) and promote **antibody production** (humoral immunity). The thymus **degenerates in old age**, so immune responses weaken.

key_terms.definition_md: Enlargement of the thyroid gland, for example from iodine deficiency.
Defective growth and development of a baby whose mother was hypothyroid in pregnancy.
A form of hyperthyroidism (Graves’ disease) with protruding eyeballs, high BMR and weight loss.
Thymus peptides that help T-lymphocytes differentiate and promote antibody production.

sections.heading: 4. Adrenal gland, pancreas and gonads
sections.body_md:
**Adrenal glands:** one at the anterior part of each kidney, with a central **medulla** and an outer **cortex**.
- **Medulla:** **adrenaline (epinephrine)** and **noradrenaline (norepinephrine)**, the **catecholamines**, secreted rapidly in stress and emergencies — **emergency hormones** or hormones of **fight or flight**. They increase alertness, cause pupillary dilation, piloerection and sweating, increase heart rate, strength of contraction and breathing rate, and stimulate breakdown of glycogen (raising blood glucose), lipids and proteins.
- **Cortex:** three layers — **zona reticularis** (inner), **zona fasciculata** (middle), **zona glomerulosa** (outer) — secreting **corticoids**. **Glucocorticoids** (e.g. **cortisol**) stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis, inhibit cellular uptake and use of amino acids, help maintain the cardiovascular system and kidney function, produce **anti-inflammatory** reactions, suppress the immune response and stimulate RBC production. **Mineralocorticoids** (mainly **aldosterone**) act on renal tubules, stimulating reabsorption of **sodium ions and water** and excretion of **potassium and phosphate ions**, maintaining electrolytes, fluid volume, osmotic pressure and blood pressure. Small amounts of **androgenic steroids** affect growth of axial, pubic and facial hair at puberty. Underproduction causes **Addison’s disease** (acute weakness and fatigue).

**Pancreas:** a **composite gland** (exocrine and endocrine). About **1 to 2 million islets of Langerhans** form only **1 to 2 percent** of the tissue. **α cells** secrete **glucagon**, a peptide that acts mainly on hepatocytes, stimulating **glycogenolysis** and **gluconeogenesis** and reducing cellular glucose uptake: it is **hyperglycaemic**. **β cells** secrete **insulin**, a peptide that acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes, enhancing glucose uptake and use and stimulating **glycogenesis**: it is **hypoglycaemic**. Prolonged hyperglycaemia causes **diabetes mellitus**, with loss of glucose in urine and formation of harmful **ketone bodies**; it is treated with insulin therapy.

**Testis:** in the scrotal sac; seminiferous tubules and interstitial tissue. **Leydig (interstitial) cells** make **androgens**, mainly **testosterone**, which regulate the male accessory sex organs, muscular growth, facial and axillary hair, aggressiveness, low-pitched voice, spermatogenesis, male sexual behaviour (libido) and anabolic effects on protein and carbohydrate metabolism.

**Ovary:** in the abdomen; one ovum per menstrual cycle. **Estrogen** from growing follicles stimulates female secondary sex organs, follicle development, female secondary sex characters (e.g. high-pitched voice), mammary gland development and female sexual behaviour. After ovulation the ruptured follicle becomes the **corpus luteum**, which secretes mainly **progesterone**: it supports pregnancy and stimulates formation of **alveoli** in the mammary glands and milk secretion.

(Blood glucose values in the graph and questions are illustrative typical values; normal ranges and the kidney threshold, often given as about 180 mg per dL, vary between people and laboratories.)

sections.heading: 5. Hormones of the heart, kidney and gastrointestinal tract
sections.body_md:
Hormones are also secreted by some tissues that are not endocrine glands.
- **Heart:** the **atrial wall** secretes **atrial natriuretic factor (ANF)**, which **decreases blood pressure**: when pressure rises, ANF dilates blood vessels.
- **Kidney:** **juxtaglomerular cells** produce the peptide **erythropoietin**, which stimulates **erythropoiesis** (formation of RBCs).
- **Gastrointestinal tract:** endocrine cells secrete four major peptide hormones. **Gastrin** acts on gastric glands, stimulating secretion of **HCl and pepsinogen**. **Secretin** acts on the exocrine pancreas, stimulating secretion of **water and bicarbonate ions**. **Cholecystokinin (CCK)** acts on the **pancreas and gall bladder**, stimulating release of pancreatic enzymes and bile juice. **Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP)** **inhibits gastric secretion and motility**.
- Several other non-endocrine tissues secrete hormones called **growth factors**, essential for normal growth, repair and regeneration.

key_terms.definition_md: A hormone of the atrial wall that dilates blood vessels and lowers blood pressure.
A kidney hormone from juxtaglomerular cells that stimulates red blood cell formation.
A gut hormone that makes the pancreas secrete water and bicarbonate ions.

sections.heading: 6. Mechanism of hormone action
sections.body_md:
Hormones act on target tissues by binding to specific proteins called **hormone receptors**, present only in the target tissues.
- **Membrane-bound receptors** lie on the cell membrane; **intracellular receptors** lie inside the cell, mostly in the nucleus (**nuclear receptors**).
- Binding forms a **hormone–receptor complex**; each receptor is **specific** to one hormone. The complex brings about biochemical changes that regulate the metabolism and functions of the target tissue.

**Chemical classes of hormones:**
1. **Peptide, polypeptide and protein hormones** — insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones.
2. **Steroids** — cortisol, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone.
3. **Iodothyronines** — thyroid hormones.
4. **Amino-acid derivatives** — epinephrine.

**Two pathways:**
- Hormones that bind **membrane-bound receptors** normally do **not enter** the target cell; they generate **second messengers** (e.g. **cyclic AMP, IP3, calcium ions**), which regulate cellular metabolism. Such cascades amplify the signal (an illustrative model: 1 × 100 × 50 = 5000 product molecules from one hormone molecule), which is one reason trace amounts suffice.
- Hormones that bind **intracellular receptors** (steroids, iodothyronines) mostly regulate **gene expression** or chromosome function through the hormone–receptor complex interacting with the **genome**.

The cumulative biochemical actions produce physiological and developmental effects.

sections.heading: 7. Disorders of the endocrine system
sections.body_md:
Both **excess** and **deficiency** of a hormone cause disease:
- **Pituitary dwarfism** — low GH in childhood; stunted growth.
- **Gigantism** — excess GH in childhood; **acromegaly** — excess GH in adults.
- **Diabetes insipidus** — impaired ADH; large volumes of urine, dehydration.
- **Goitre and cretinism** — hypothyroidism (often iodine deficiency); **exophthalmic goitre (Graves’ disease)** — hyperthyroidism.
- **Addison’s disease** — underproduction of adrenal cortex hormones; acute weakness and fatigue.
- **Diabetes mellitus** — prolonged hyperglycaemia from lack of insulin action; glucose in urine, ketone bodies; treated with insulin.

key_terms.definition_md: Acute weakness and fatigue from underproduction of adrenal cortex hormones.
Prolonged hyperglycaemia with glucose in the urine and ketone bodies, from lack of insulin action.
Harmful compounds formed in untreated diabetes mellitus.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying oxytocin and vasopressin are made in the posterior pituitary (they are made in the hypothalamus and only stored and released there).
- Confusing diabetes insipidus (ADH) with diabetes mellitus (insulin).
- Writing glycogenesis for glucagon or glycogenolysis for insulin.
- Calling PTH hypocalcaemic (it raises blood calcium).
- Listing the cortex zones in the wrong order (outside to inside: glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis).
- Saying steroid hormones act through cyclic AMP (they bind intracellular receptors and change gene expression).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: name a hormone, gland, cell type, zone or disorder.
- 2–3-mark answers: hypothalamic control of the pituitary; thyroid functions; emergency hormones; insulin and glucagon; gut hormones; two kinds of diabetes.
- 5-mark answers: the pituitary; thyroid and parathyroid; adrenal and pancreas; mechanism of hormone action.
- Case-based items: glucose tolerance data, iodine deficiency surveys, stress responses or receptor experiments, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: Which statement matches the present scientific definition of a hormone?

options.text_md: A digestive enzyme carried to its site of action through a duct
A nutrient stored in the liver and released when needed
A non-nutrient chemical that acts as an intercellular messenger and is produced in trace amounts
Any secretion of a gland, with or without a duct

questions.solution_md: Hormones are non-nutrient chemicals which act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In an animal experiment, a harmless dye is injected into the capillary bed at the base of the hypothalamus. Through the hypophysial portal veins it reaches capillaries in which region first?

options.text_md: The anterior pituitary (pars distalis)
The posterior pituitary (pars nervosa)
The pineal gland
The thyroid gland

questions.solution_md: The portal circulatory system links the hypothalamus with the anterior pituitary, carrying releasing and inhibiting hormones to it — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Somatostatin, a hypothalamic hormone, acts on the pituitary to

options.text_md: stimulate the release of gonadotrophins
stimulate milk ejection
inhibit the release of melatonin
inhibit the release of growth hormone

questions.solution_md: Somatostatin is an inhibiting hormone: it inhibits the release of growth hormone from the pituitary — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The only hormone secreted by the pars intermedia acts on

options.text_md: the uterus, causing contraction
melanocytes, regulating skin pigmentation
the kidney tubules, conserving water
the thyroid, stimulating its secretion

questions.solution_md: The pars intermedia secretes MSH, which acts on melanocytes and regulates skin pigmentation — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student writes: “Oxytocin and vasopressin are made by the posterior pituitary.” Which correction is accurate?

options.text_md: They are made by the anterior pituitary and stored in the hypothalamus.
They are made by the pars intermedia and released by the pineal gland.
They are made by hypothalamic neurons, carried down their axons and only stored and released by the posterior pituitary.
They are made in the kidney and stored in the posterior pituitary.

questions.solution_md: The neurohypophysis stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin, which are synthesised by the hypothalamus and transported axonally — option (c).

questions.stem_md: After a head injury that damaged the hypothalamus and pituitary stalk, a man passes very large volumes of dilute urine and is always thirsty, but his blood glucose is normal. The most likely cause is

options.text_md: lack of insulin, causing diabetes mellitus
excess aldosterone, causing salt retention
reduced release of vasopressin (ADH), causing diabetes insipidus
excess thyroxine, causing a high metabolic rate

questions.solution_md: Without ADH the kidney cannot conserve water, so water is lost and the body dehydrates: diabetes insipidus. Normal glucose rules out diabetes mellitus — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Over ten years, a 46-year-old woman notices that her rings and shoes no longer fit and her jaw and facial features have become coarse. Tests show a pituitary tumour. Her condition is

options.text_md: acromegaly, from excess growth hormone in adulthood
gigantism, from excess growth hormone in childhood
pituitary dwarfism, from too little growth hormone
cretinism, from too little thyroid hormone

questions.solution_md: Excess growth hormone in adults, especially in middle age, causes severe disfigurement, especially of the face: acromegaly. It is slow and often goes undetected for years — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An eight-year-old boy is much shorter than his classmates, but his body proportions and intelligence are normal. Blood tests show low growth hormone. The likely diagnosis is

options.text_md: acromegaly
Addison’s disease
exophthalmic goitre
pituitary dwarfism

questions.solution_md: Low secretion of growth hormone in childhood results in stunted growth called pituitary dwarfism — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A nurse who moves to night shifts finds that her sleep–wake cycle and body temperature rhythm are disturbed. The hormone most closely linked to these daily rhythms is

options.text_md: prolactin, from the anterior pituitary
melatonin, from the pineal gland
thymosin, from the thymus
aldosterone, from the adrenal cortex

questions.solution_md: Melatonin plays a very important role in regulating the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm, such as the sleep–wake cycle and body temperature — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a hill district where the soil and water are poor in iodine, many adults have a visible swelling at the front of the neck. The swelling is best explained as

options.text_md: an enlarged thymus caused by infection
swollen parathyroid glands caused by excess calcium
goitre, an enlarged thyroid caused by iodine deficiency and hypothyroidism
acromegaly caused by excess growth hormone

questions.solution_md: Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis; its deficiency causes hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid, called goitre — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A pregnant woman has hypothyroidism that is not treated. Which outcome is her baby at risk of?

options.text_md: Gigantism: abnormally rapid growth of the whole body
Cretinism: stunted growth, mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism
Diabetes insipidus: loss of large volumes of urine
Graves’ disease: protruding eyeballs and weight loss

questions.solution_md: Hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development and maturation of the growing baby, leading to cretinism — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A 30-year-old man has an enlarged thyroid, protruding eyeballs, a raised basal metabolic rate and weight loss despite eating well. His condition is

options.text_md: exophthalmic goitre (Graves’ disease), a form of hyperthyroidism
simple goitre caused by iodine deficiency
cretinism caused by hypothyroidism
Addison’s disease caused by adrenal failure

questions.solution_md: Enlarged thyroid, protrusion of the eyeballs, increased BMR and weight loss characterise exophthalmic goitre, also called Graves’ disease — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is NOT an effect of parathyroid hormone?

options.text_md: It stimulates bone resorption (demineralisation).
It stimulates the deposition of calcium in bones.
It stimulates reabsorption of calcium ions by the renal tubules.
It increases absorption of calcium from digested food.

questions.solution_md: PTH raises blood calcium: it stimulates bone resorption, renal reabsorption and intestinal absorption of calcium. Depositing calcium in bone would lower blood calcium — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Why do the immune responses of old people usually become weaker?

options.text_md: The pineal gland enlarges and makes too much melatonin.
The thyroid stops making thyrocalcitonin.
The thymus degenerates, so less thymosin is made and fewer T-lymphocytes differentiate.
The adrenal medulla secretes more adrenaline.

questions.solution_md: The thymus degenerates in old individuals, reducing thymosins, which are needed for T-lymphocyte differentiation and antibody production — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which change is NOT brought about by adrenaline and noradrenaline during an emergency?

options.text_md: Increased heart rate and strength of contraction
Constriction of the pupils
Breakdown of glycogen, raising blood glucose
Raising of hairs (piloerection) and sweating

questions.solution_md: The catecholamines cause pupillary dilation, not constriction, along with the other changes listed — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A doctor prescribes a cortisol-like cream for a patch of red, swollen, itchy skin. Which property of glucocorticoids is being used?

options.text_md: They stimulate the reabsorption of sodium ions in the kidney.
They stimulate the formation of melanin in the skin.
They act as second messengers inside skin cells.
They produce anti-inflammatory reactions and suppress the immune response.

questions.solution_md: Glucocorticoids, particularly cortisol, produce anti-inflammatory reactions and suppress the immune response — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Underproduction of hormones by the adrenal cortex alters carbohydrate metabolism and causes acute weakness and fatigue. This disease is called

options.text_md: Addison’s disease
Graves’ disease
diabetes insipidus
acromegaly

questions.solution_md: Addison’s disease results from underproduction of adrenal cortex hormones — option (a).

questions.stem_md: After an overnight fast, a girl’s blood glucose stays steady although she has eaten nothing for twelve hours. Which hormone mainly prevents it from falling, and how?

options.text_md: Glucagon, by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in liver cells
Insulin, by moving glucose into fat cells
Thyrocalcitonin, by releasing glucose from bones
Oxytocin, by stimulating glucose release from muscles

questions.solution_md: Glucagon acts mainly on hepatocytes, stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so it raises blood glucose — option (a).

questions.stem_md: During a medical check-up, a man’s blood pressure is found to be much higher than usual. Which hormone would his atrial walls secrete in response, and with what effect?

options.text_md: Erythropoietin, which raises the number of red blood cells
Vasopressin, which constricts vessels and raises blood pressure further
Aldosterone, which retains sodium and water
Atrial natriuretic factor, which dilates blood vessels and lowers blood pressure

questions.solution_md: When blood pressure rises, the atrial wall secretes ANF, which dilates blood vessels and reduces blood pressure — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A patient with long-standing kidney damage becomes anaemic even though his diet is adequate. Lack of which hormone best explains the anaemia?

options.text_md: Thymosin from the thymus
Erythropoietin from the juxtaglomerular cells
Gastrin from the stomach
Melatonin from the pineal gland

questions.solution_md: Juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney produce erythropoietin, which stimulates erythropoiesis (formation of red blood cells) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Acidic food from the stomach enters the duodenum. Which gut hormone then makes the exocrine pancreas release water and bicarbonate ions?

options.text_md: Gastrin
Secretin
Gastric inhibitory peptide
Insulin

questions.solution_md: Secretin acts on the exocrine pancreas and stimulates secretion of water and bicarbonate ions — option (b).

questions.stem_md: TSH travels in the blood to every organ, yet it stimulates only the thyroid. The best explanation is that

options.text_md: TSH is destroyed in all other organs
blood reaches only the thyroid in large amounts
TSH enters every cell but acts only in the thyroid nucleus
only thyroid cells carry receptors specific for TSH

questions.solution_md: Hormones act only on target tissues that carry their specific receptors; each receptor is specific to one hormone — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which hormone normally acts on its target cell through a second messenger, without entering the cell?

options.text_md: Glucagon
Cortisol
Progesterone
Thyroxine

questions.solution_md: Glucagon is a peptide hormone that binds a membrane-bound receptor and acts through second messengers; steroids and iodothyronines bind intracellular receptors — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a cell-culture study, a hormone passes through the plasma membrane, binds a receptor in the nucleus and, a few hours later, new proteins appear. The hormone is most likely

options.text_md: insulin
adrenaline
testosterone
glucagon

questions.solution_md: Steroid hormones such as testosterone interact with intracellular (nuclear) receptors and regulate gene expression — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which hormone is correctly matched with its chemical nature?

options.text_md: Insulin — steroid
Cortisol — iodothyronine
Estradiol — protein
Epinephrine — amino-acid derivative

questions.solution_md: Epinephrine is an amino-acid derivative; insulin is a peptide, cortisol and estradiol are steroids — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Why does glucose appear in the urine of a person with untreated diabetes mellitus but not in that of a healthy person?

options.text_md: Prolonged high blood glucose exceeds what the kidney tubules can reabsorb, so the extra glucose stays in the urine.
The kidney makes glucose when insulin is absent.
Glucagon is excreted in the urine and turns into glucose.
Healthy kidneys do not filter any glucose from the blood.

questions.solution_md: In diabetes mellitus prolonged hyperglycaemia leads to loss of glucose through urine, because the filtered load exceeds tubular reabsorption — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Vasopressin is also called the anti-diuretic hormone.

**Reason (R):** Vasopressin stimulates reabsorption of water and electrolytes by the distal tubules and so reduces the loss of water through urine.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; reducing diuresis is exactly why vasopressin is called ADH — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Adrenaline raises the concentration of glucose in the blood.

**Reason (R):** Adrenaline increases the heart rate and the strength of heart contraction.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but A is explained by adrenaline stimulating the breakdown of glycogen, not by its effect on the heart — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Insulin lowers the blood glucose level.

**Reason (R):** Insulin stimulates the breakdown of glycogen in liver cells.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: insulin stimulates glycogenesis (glucose to glycogen) and glucose uptake; glycogenolysis is stimulated by glucagon — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Steroid hormones act on their target cells by generating cyclic AMP as a second messenger.

**Reason (R):** Steroid hormones interact with intracellular receptors and mostly regulate gene expression.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: second messengers are used by hormones that bind membrane-bound receptors. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lack of iodine in the diet can lead to an enlarged thyroid gland.

**Reason (R):** Iodine is essential for the normal rate of synthesis of thyroid hormones.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; without iodine hormone synthesis falls (hypothyroidism) and the gland enlarges as goitre — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In humans, the pars intermedia is almost merged with the pars distalis.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Glucagon is a hypoglycaemic hormone.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Glucagon raises blood glucose, so it is a hyperglycaemic hormone; insulin is hypoglycaemic.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Hormones that bind membrane-bound receptors normally enter the target cell before they act.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. They normally do not enter the cell; they generate second messengers that regulate cell metabolism.

questions.stem_md: The pituitary gland lies in a bony cavity of the skull called the sella ______.
questions.solution_md: Turcica: the pituitary is located in the sella turcica and is attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk.

questions.stem_md: The innermost layer of the adrenal cortex is the zona ______.
questions.solution_md: Reticularis: from inside out the layers are zona reticularis, zona fasciculata and zona glomerulosa.

questions.stem_md: Because it raises the calcium level of the blood, parathyroid hormone is described as a ______ hormone.
questions.solution_md: Hypercalcaemic (hypercalcemic).

questions.stem_md: Match each hormone (column I) with the cells or tissue that secrete it (column II).

options.text_md: Testosterone
Progesterone
Insulin
Erythropoietin

match_right.text_md: β cells of the islets of Langerhans

questions.stem_md: Describe the parts of the human pituitary gland and the hormones each part secretes or releases, with their actions. How does abnormal growth hormone secretion affect the body?

answer.model_answer_md:
The pituitary lies in the **sella turcica** and is attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk. It has an **adenohypophysis** (pars distalis and pars intermedia) and a **neurohypophysis** (pars nervosa).

**Pars distalis (anterior pituitary):** **GH** promotes growth; **prolactin** regulates growth of mammary glands and milk formation; **TSH** stimulates the thyroid; **ACTH** stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete glucocorticoids; **LH and FSH** (gonadotrophins) stimulate the gonads — LH causes androgen secretion and ovulation and maintains the corpus luteum, while FSH and androgens regulate spermatogenesis and FSH stimulates follicle growth.

**Pars intermedia:** **MSH** regulates skin pigmentation through melanocytes; in humans it is almost merged with the pars distalis.

**Neurohypophysis:** stores and releases **oxytocin**, which contracts the uterus at childbirth and causes milk ejection, and **vasopressin (ADH)**, which makes distal tubules reabsorb water; both are made in the hypothalamus.

**GH disorders:** excess in childhood causes **gigantism**, deficiency causes **pituitary dwarfism**, and excess in middle age causes **acromegaly**, with facial disfigurement.

questions.stem_md: Describe the thyroid and parathyroid glands: their position, the hormones they secrete and their functions. Explain two disorders caused by abnormal thyroid activity.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Thyroid.** Two lobes lie on either side of the trachea, joined by an isthmus. The gland is made of follicles and stromal tissue. Follicular cells synthesise **thyroxine (tetraiodothyronine, T4)** and **triiodothyronine (T3)**, which need **iodine**. They regulate the **basal metabolic rate**, support red blood cell formation, control the metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, and maintain water and electrolyte balance. The thyroid also secretes **thyrocalcitonin**, which regulates blood calcium.

**Parathyroid.** Four glands lie on the back of the thyroid, one pair in each lobe. They secrete **parathyroid hormone**, regulated by blood calcium. PTH is **hypercalcaemic**: it stimulates bone resorption, renal reabsorption of calcium and absorption of calcium from food; with TCT it maintains calcium balance.

**Disorders.** **Iodine deficiency** causes **hypothyroidism and goitre**; in pregnancy hypothyroidism causes **cretinism** in the baby (stunted growth, mental retardation, deaf-mutism), and in adult women irregular menstrual cycles. **Hyperthyroidism**, from thyroid cancer or nodules, raises hormone levels; **exophthalmic goitre (Graves’ disease)** shows an enlarged thyroid, protruding eyeballs, raised BMR and weight loss.

questions.stem_md: Describe the hormones of the adrenal gland and of the endocrine pancreas. Explain how the pancreatic hormones keep blood glucose within limits and what happens when this control fails.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Adrenal medulla:** **adrenaline and noradrenaline** (catecholamines) are emergency hormones. They raise alertness, heart rate, strength of contraction and breathing rate, dilate pupils, cause sweating and piloerection, and stimulate breakdown of glycogen, lipids and proteins.

**Adrenal cortex** (zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis): **glucocorticoids** such as cortisol stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis, are anti-inflammatory and suppress immunity; **mineralocorticoids** such as aldosterone conserve sodium and water and excrete potassium; small amounts of **androgens** affect hair growth at puberty. Underproduction causes **Addison’s disease**.

**Endocrine pancreas:** about 1 to 2 million **islets of Langerhans**. **α cells** secrete **glucagon**, which acts on hepatocytes, stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so blood glucose rises. **β cells** secrete **insulin**, which makes hepatocytes and adipocytes take up and use glucose and stimulates glycogenesis, so blood glucose falls. Their opposing actions maintain **glucose homeostasis**.

**Failure:** prolonged hyperglycaemia causes **diabetes mellitus**, with loss of glucose in urine and harmful **ketone bodies**; it is treated with insulin therapy.

questions.stem_md: Explain the mechanism of hormone action. Include hormone receptors, the chemical classes of hormones, and the two main pathways by which hormones change the activity of target cells.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Receptors.** A hormone acts only on target tissues that carry its **hormone receptors**. Receptors on the cell membrane are **membrane-bound**; those inside the cell are **intracellular**, mostly nuclear. Each receptor is **specific** to one hormone. Binding forms a **hormone–receptor complex**, which causes biochemical changes that regulate the metabolism and functions of the target tissue.

**Chemical classes.** (i) Peptide, polypeptide and protein hormones such as insulin, glucagon and the pituitary and hypothalamic hormones; (ii) steroids such as cortisol, testosterone, estradiol and progesterone; (iii) iodothyronines (thyroid hormones); (iv) amino-acid derivatives such as epinephrine.

**Pathway 1:** hormones that bind **membrane-bound receptors** (peptides, proteins, amino-acid derivatives) normally do not enter the cell. They generate **second messengers** such as **cyclic AMP, IP3 and calcium ions**, which regulate cell metabolism, often by activating enzymes.

**Pathway 2:** hormones that bind **intracellular receptors** (steroids, iodothyronines) form a complex that interacts with the **genome**, regulating **gene expression** or chromosome function.

The cumulative biochemical actions produce physiological and developmental effects.

questions.solution_md: Receptors, classes, two pathways.

questions.stem_md: A fitness website claims: “Hormones are basically enzymes, they act on every cell they reach, and taking more of a hormone always makes the body work better.” Evaluate each part of this claim, using examples of hormone action and of disorders caused by excess or deficiency.

answer.model_answer_md:
**“Hormones are enzymes.”** Incorrect. Hormones are **non-nutrient chemical messengers** produced in **trace amounts**; they belong to several chemical classes — peptides and proteins (insulin), steroids (cortisol), iodothyronines (thyroxine) and amino-acid derivatives (adrenaline). They do not catalyse reactions themselves; they change the activity of target cells, sometimes by activating enzymes through second messengers.

**“They act on every cell.”** Incorrect. A hormone acts only where its **specific receptors** are present. TSH reaches every organ in the blood but acts only on the thyroid; glucagon acts mainly on hepatocytes.

**“More is always better.”** Incorrect. The body needs the **right amount**, regulated by feedback. Excess growth hormone causes **gigantism** in children and **acromegaly** in adults; excess thyroid hormone causes **hyperthyroidism**, as in Graves’ disease with weight loss and raised BMR. Too little is also harmful: GH deficiency causes **dwarfism**, insulin deficiency causes **diabetes mellitus**, and adrenal cortex failure causes **Addison’s disease**.

**Judgement.** All three parts are wrong. Hormones are specific, finely balanced messengers, and both excess and deficiency cause disease, so hormones should be taken only under medical advice.
